title: Retrieval grounding
point: Retrieve a bounded set of sourced chunks and let the answer claim only what those chunks support: no source, no claim.
definition: Retrieval grounding fetches the top-k chunks for a query, bounded by a token budget, each tagged with a source id and a timestamp. The answer cites the chunks it relies on and makes no claim that no chunk supports.

objective.text: Given a question and a set of retrieved chunks, decide which claims the answer may make, attach the right citations, and say what to do when no chunk supports an answer.

misconceptions.correction: Retrieval only supplies evidence. The model can still ignore it or add claims, so require a citation for each claim and check that the cited chunk supports it.

misconceptions.claim: Retrieving more chunks always gives better answers.
misconceptions.correction: Extra chunks cost tokens and add distracting near-misses. Bound k by the token budget and tune it against a measured eval set.

l1: Split documents into chunks, index them, and at query time retrieve the top k most relevant. Bound k by tokens, such as 10 chunks of 400 tokens within a 4,000-token budget.
Each chunk carries a source id and a timestamp, such as the article id and its last update date. The answer cites the ids of the chunks it uses.
No source, no claim. If no retrieved chunk supports a statement, the answer leaves it out or says the information was not found.
l2: A user asks whether they can return opened headphones. Retrieval returns three chunks: the returns policy updated in May, a shipping article and a returns policy from 2024.
The current policy says opened audio products can be returned within 14 days if unused. The answer states that and cites the May policy chunk by its id.
The 2024 chunk says 30 days. Its older timestamp lets the answer prefer the current version, and the conflict is logged so the content owners can retire the old page.
l3: Measure retrieval and grounding separately. Recall at k asks whether the right chunk was retrieved; faithfulness asks whether each claim is supported by a cited chunk.
Suppose recall at 10 is 92 per cent on a 500-question eval set. Then 40 questions never see the right chunk, and no prompt change can fix those 40.
Raising k to 15 adds 2,000 tokens, or $0.004 per call at $2 per million. Make that change only if the eval shows recall rising enough to justify the cost.
